access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.rules: Respect private timberland access rules; pack it in/pack it out. The upper route and summit lie within the federally designated Mount Baker Wilderness — no bikes or mechanized travel once inside the wilderness boundary.
access.permit: None required — a self-issue climbing register may exist at some trailheads but is optional and free.
access.closures: Logging-road access may be gated, permitted, or closed during active forestry operations, or change with the current landowner.
access.landManager: Upper route and summit lie within Mount Baker Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Ranger District); the lower approach crosses private industrial timberland.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.
access.passRequired: No federal pass is required at the private logging-road gate itself; verify current landowner rules before the trip, since some past owners have required a signed waiver or day-use permission.

overnight_permit.where: Camping is on unregulated Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and private timberland; no wilderness permit or registration is needed. The Dailey Prairie logging-road gate is separately locked to vehicles by the timber company, which is an access issue unrelated to camping.

before.permit: No climbing permit; the approach crosses private and DNR timberland - check current access, and carry a Discover Pass where parking on DNR land.
what_to_bring: Weyerhaeuser day-use recreation permit (confirm/purchase before driving out)
GPX track or a detailed written road-fork description - the logging-road maze is the single biggest cause of lost time
Mountain bike, to cut hours off the ~5-6 mile road approach
Plenty of water - little to no reliable water source once you leave the lower road system
pro_tips: The dunite rock offers superb friction — trust your feet
Confirm current logging-road access before the trip; gates and conditions change
Most parties mountain-bike the ~5 miles of lower logging road to save time and energy (bikes must be left before entering the Wilderness boundary)

This approach crosses private industrial timberland (most recently reported by climbers as Hampton Family Forests, formerly Olivine Corp./Weyerhaeuser) — a fee recreational permit is required, administered via MyOutdoorAgent.com; call ahead, since the access gate has a history of being locked without notice.
Stay left (west side) of the ridge crest near the false summits — straying right leads into harder, looser, exposed terrain.

road.name: Mosquito Lake Road to Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack)
road.driveNote: Roads cross private industrial timberland whose ownership has changed hands over the years (most recently reported by climbers as Hampton Family Forests); gate locations, mileage, and any permission requirements can change without notice — verify current status from recent trip reports before driving. Many parties bike the lower logging-road miles to save time.
road.seasonalGate: Gates and access vary with forestry activity and current ownership; check recent trip reports before a visit.

pitch_detail.notes: Gated logging roads (bike-friendly) to roughly 4,900 ft, then a use trail through clearcut and timber to a fire ring near treeline
Ridge-crest scrambling through scattered fir stands on solid, high-friction dunite, marked by occasional cairns

Exposed scrambling past the Obelisk and Cockscomb rock features to the summit; some parties rope up for a short mixed step on the variation start, and there is a bypass notch ('Katie Gap') around 6,300 ft

sectionBreakdown.note: Done in a single day, no camp. From the gated bridge trailhead (~1,200 ft) parties bike/hike ~5-6 miles of logging road to the ridge toe, then climb ~1 mile and ~1,500 vertical ft …

before.descent_text: Reverse the West Ridge to the approach; the friction rock makes downclimbing straightforward. In early season (roughly May-June), many parties instead glissade a long, steep snowfield on the north slope and traverse back to rejoin the West Ridge trail near 4,600 ft.
before.best_season: Snow typically clears the West Ridge by mid-to-late June in an average year. The north-face glissade descent option is best taken in June-July, before it degrades to loose scree; July-September gives the driest rock and easiest road/bike access. By October, early snow, shorter days, and worse road conditions add real risk to the long approach.
before.overview: North Twin Sister (6,644 ft) is the second-highest and most-visited summit of the Twin Sisters Range, a striking massif of dunite (an ultramafic, olivine-rich mantle rock) about 10 miles southwest of Mount Baker. Dunite is exposed at the surface in only a handful of places worldwide, and here it weathers to a reddish-orange rind while staying grippy, sandpaper-textured stone underneath - the reason the West Ridge has a reputation as some of the best rock scrambling in the state. A small glacier clings to the peak's northeast slopes. Both Twin Sisters summits sit near, but the approach roads lie outside, the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest boundary, crossing private timberland whose access policy has shifted repeatedly over the decades.

hazards: Glacier/crevasse proximity near the North-South saddle if the line passes close to the Sisters Glacier's upper apron
Unpredictable timing of snow bridges near the saddle - safest earlier in summer, riskier as crevasses open later in the season
Complex private logging-road approach shared with the West Ridge route - see that route for navigation notes
Unpredictable gate closures on private timberland access
gear: Approach shoes with sticky rubber for the olivine scrambling
Ice axe (and possibly crampons) if the line passes near residual snow/glacier terrain on the saddle
before.best_season: July-September is the reliable window. If your line to the summit passes near the North-South saddle above the Sisters Glacier, earlier season (before crevasses open later in summer) is generally safer for that terrain - check recent trip reports for current glacier/snow-bridge conditions before committing.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed as a standalone objective; most likely attempted by parties combining it with a South Twin traverse or seeking a quieter alternative to the West Ridge, July-September weekends
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Unknown - low-traffic relative to the standard West Ridge; this between-summits approach is far less represented in trip-report archives than the West Ridge route, suggesting it sees a small fraction of that traffic

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long day given the remote timberland-road approach; expect a full car-to-car day with significant mileage before the scrambling even begins
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light alpine day pack — helmet recommended for slab/rockfall exposure; carry extra contingency (food/layers) given the remote, gated access

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long and variable depending on current gate closures on the timberland road network; plan for a long full day with no guarantee of vehicle access all the way to a standard trailhead
requiredSkills: Class 3 scrambling on steep dunite/olivine slabs
route-finding on the ridge between the two summits
navigating/driving or biking a remote, potentially gated timberland-road network
handling lingering snow on approach or route in early season
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced Class 3 scrambler with strong self-sufficiency — the combination of a long remote approach, gated/uncertain timberland roads, and steep slab terrain means this suits a partner used to route-finding without a well-established trail or published consensus

approach_logistics.trailhead: Clearwater Creek gate (Middle Fork Nooksack logging roads)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the gate before the Clearwater Creek / Middle Fork Nooksack crossing

before.approach: Drive to the gate before the Clearwater Creek/Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on the logging-road network west of Mosquito Lake Road. From the gate, the approach is entirely on old logging roads and then ridge/brush for roughly 6-6.5 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car-to-summit, one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble — most parties mountain-bike the road portion to save time and legs. Cross the bridge over Clearwater Creek and ascend the well-graded logging road for about 2.5 miles; at the first major fork stay right (the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry). About 0.2 miles later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the left branch here. Around the 5-mile mark, near a dirt mound and a cairn, leave the logging road proper and pick up an old, overgrown road spur that switchbacks up through a clearcut; this is the point where route-finding gets harder and the brush thickens noticeably (expect to get soaked in wet weather — the clearcut brush is notorious for saturating pants and boots even without rain). By about 6.4 miles you pass an old fire-ring in the clearcut and enter a final band of brush before reaching timber at the base of the west ridge; from there, follow the timbered ridge itself up to where it opens onto rock and the class 3 scrambling begins. There is no reliable water source once you leave Clearwater Creek near the trailhead, so carry what you need for the day. In low cloud/fog, which is common on the Twin Sisters, the clearcut and lower-ridge sections lack obvious cairns or a defined tread and route-finding can be genuinely difficult; parties should be comfortable navigating by map/GPS through brushy, featureless clearcut terrain. On the ridge proper, cairns mark a Class 3 line — the key beta repeated across trip reports is to stay LEFT (climber's left) on the crest; drifting right leads toward false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 terrain on loose, exposed rock.

approach_variants.name: Clearwater Creek gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive to the gate before the Clearwater Creek / Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on the logging-road network west of Mosquito Lake Road. From the gate it is roughly 6-6.5 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over Clearwater Creek and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay RIGHT; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the LEFT branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right on the crest into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after Clearwater Creek near the gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRT MOUND AND CAIRN AT ABOUT MILE 5 IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER ON THIS APPROACH, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE NAVIGATION GETS HARD. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — RIGHT at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then LEFT at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

THE FIRE RING AT ABOUT MILE 6.4 IS THE SECOND MARKER, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

IN LOW CLOUD, WHICH IS NORMAL HERE, THE CLEARCUT IS THE HARDEST GROUND ON THE ROUTE AND IT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

THE ONE PIECE OF BETA THAT REPEATS IN EVERY ACCOUNT, AND IT IS THE FOG TEST FOR THE RIDGE ITSELF: STAY LEFT — CLIMBER'S LEFT — ON THE CREST. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting RIGHT leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT RANGE. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.notes:
The other documented way onto the same ridge, from the other side of the road network: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap on the ridge crest
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROAD NETWORK IS THE CRUX AND THE MOUNTAIN IS NOT. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. THE END OF RIDEABLE ROAD IS THE MARKER, and on this network it is commonly identified by a LARGE CULVERT PIPE at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot. THE CLIMBERS' PATH IS BRUSHY AND WET AND NOT HARD TO FOLLOW — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest. ARRIVAL: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. On the crest, STAY CLIMBER'S LEFT; drifting right puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground. WHICH SISTER AM I ON? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. NORTH TWIN's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. SOUTH TWIN's west ridge is gained at an obvious NOTCH in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.

waypoints.name: Gated Bridge Trailhead (FR 38 / Weyerhaeuser Rd 9000)
waypoints.note: Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack (reached via Mosquito Lake Rd from Acme, then FR 38/Dailey Quarry Rd); gate is usually closed and a Weyerhaeuser recreation permit is posted as required — bike or hike the logging roads from here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue on Forest Road 38. Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge, at around 1,200 feet — the gate is usually closed and posts a required Weyerhaeuser recreation permit. The road beyond is private timberland and access can change from year to year, so confirm the gate status before your trip.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie road-to-trail transition
waypoints.note: Logging roads climb roughly 2,000 ft over the first 5 miles to Dailey Prairie, a wet clearcut-plateau meadow, where the singletrack climbers' trail for the West Ridge route branches off the road.

waypoints.name: Bike stash / treeline
waypoints.note: Switchbacking trail through old logging spurs reaches treeline near 4,100 ft, marked by a firepit and cairn where parties stash bikes and continue on foot up onto the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Katie Gap
waypoints.note: Notch where the cairned crest route dead-ends at cliffs; climbers drop through this gap to bypass the obstacle — the route's well-known routefinding crux, easy to miss in poor visibility.

waypoints.name: Summit headwall scramble
waypoints.note: Final stretch of sustained Class 3, locally Class 4, scrambling on grippy but exposed orange dunite (olivine); loose blocks and multiple false summits above this point.

waypoints.name: North Twin Sister summit
waypoints.note: True north summit of the Twin Sisters Range; broad views of Mount Baker, the San Juan Islands, and across the connecting ridge to South Twin (7,000+ ft).
